summary: Defines mechanisms for privacy in SIP. It gives guidelines for building messages that do not reveal personal identity information, defines a privacy service role for intermediaries, and lets users ask for particular privacy functions. It handles needs that user agents cannot satisfy themselves.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3323 defines ways to limit identity information in Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) messages. A user agent can hide some details itself, while a network privacy service handles information that must remain usable for routing.

subtitle: How SIP users request privacy and how intermediaries can remove identifying information.

tldr.problem: SIP messages can reveal a caller through several identity and routing fields. A user agent cannot always hide those fields without breaking later message routing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the Privacy header and a privacy-service role for intermediaries that can remove or replace information the user agent cannot safely change.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism separates user-provided, header, and session privacy. Network-provided privacy requires trust in the service, and session privacy without end-to-end media security is not recommended.

today: RFC 3323 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2002. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Where SIP Can Reveal Identity
sections.content:
SIP privacy means withholding a person's identity or related information from one or more parties in a dialog. Identity can appear in the From and To fields, but also in Contact, Via, Record-Route, Call-ID, and other headers. Some of these fields reveal a provider or network as well as a person.

Some fields are needed to route later messages in the dialog, so a user agent cannot simply replace them with unusable values. The RFC defines ways for users to request help from intermediaries while allowing recipients or intermediaries to reject requests whose sender cannot be identified.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP messages can reveal identity in more places than the caller-name field. Some identifying fields also help route later messages, so hiding them can require network assistance.

sections.title: User and Network Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC describes user-provided privacy and two forms of network-provided privacy: header privacy and session privacy. A user agent can omit optional identifying headers, use anonymous values, or protect message contents. An intermediary can remove information that the user agent cannot change without disrupting routing.

Direct end-to-end signaling cannot conceal the participants' network addresses from each other. A user should also consider that an intermediary may not provide the requested privacy, and some recipients may reject requests from unidentified users.
sections.plainLanguage: A user agent can hide details that are optional. A network service is needed for information that must remain functional for routing or media delivery.

sections.title: Building a Private SIP Message
sections.content:
User agents SHOULD omit optional headers that reveal personal information and SHOULD use anonymous values where appropriate. The RFC recommends the display name “Anonymous” and the hostname anonymous.invalid for anonymous URIs. The From field must still contain a valid, unique tag.

Contact and Via values help route later messages, so a user agent SHOULD NOT alter their host portion for privacy. If these fields need anonymizing, the user can request a privacy service. A user agent can also replace a Call-ID value that may contain its host name or IP address with a random value.
sections.plainLanguage: A user agent can remove optional identifying fields and use an anonymous From value. It should leave routing fields usable and ask a privacy service to hide them when needed.

sections.title: The Privacy Header
sections.content:
The Privacy header lets a user agent request particular handling. The values include header for obscuring identifying headers, session for anonymizing session media, user for network-provided user-level functions, none for no privacy functions, and critical when failure to provide the requested functions should cause rejection.

A header may contain none by itself, or one or more of user, header, and session, optionally followed by critical. If critical is present and the service cannot provide all requested functions, it must reject the request with a 500 response.
sections.plainLanguage: The Privacy header states which information a network service should hide. The critical value asks the service to reject the request if it cannot provide the requested privacy.

sections.title: Privacy Service and Its Limits
sections.content:
A privacy service is an intermediary role that supplies privacy functions a user agent cannot provide. For header privacy, it may replace Contact values, remove earlier Via fields, and store the original routing values so it can restore them for later messages. For session privacy, it acts as a back-to-back user agent and controls a middlebox that hides the apparent source of media traffic.

Network-provided privacy requires substantial trust in the service. The service can see information it removes, and downstream parties can trace anonymous messages to that service. Session privacy without end-to-end protection for the media is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: A privacy service changes messages on the user's behalf and may need to remember original routing details. Users must trust it, especially when it can access session media.

viz.caption: VALUES FOR THE SIP PRIVACY HEADER

items.label: Header privacy
items.desc: Obscure identifying headers that the user agent cannot safely change.

items.label: Session privacy
items.desc: Anonymize the apparent source of session media.

items.label: User privacy
items.desc: Ask the network to perform user-level privacy functions.

items.label: Critical
items.desc: Reject the request if requested services cannot be provided.
